claims_guardrails: No source, no verdict: every on-screen number quoted from AS/TC; show n wherever a small-sample number appears.

Falsifiability = B06: plain 0.996 AND non-empty 0.933 AND n=4 shown together; rule-based control stays 1.000. Verdict provisional (n=4), pending --chapters 19-27 (NOT run — show as 'next', never a result).
Not 'LLM bad' — precision/recall trade-off, no gold standard. Model named exactly (qwen2.5-coder:7b, temp 0, pinned, digest). Difficulty 0.350 / MAE 0.88 = weakest signal / faculty-calibration.
Side-by-side at comparison (rule-based col vs qwen col), held >=2s. No learning/efficacy claim. Divergence on fuzzy fields = faculty-review agenda (continuity w/ week-02).

beats.narration_text: Hello, fellows. The method paper flagged an honest worry: an AI tagger is stochastic — run it twice, get different tags. So can you trust it? Rather than argue, we ran the ablation. The real question: does the fancy tagger earn its place, or does the cheap, deterministic one already do the job?

props.segment: Does the Fancy Part Earn It?
props.command: The paper worried an AI tagger is stochastic — run it twice, get different tags. So we ran the ablation: deterministic rule-based vs a pinned open model. Does the fancy tagger earn its place?
output: Rule-based: exactly reproducible (1.000). Pinned LLM at temp 0: ~0.991.
They agree most on the field that matters — materials (Jaccard 0.89).
Verdict: ship the deterministic default. (Strongest number rests on n≈4.)

beats.narration_text: First — how to read an ablation, in five checks. One, isolate: change exactly one thing. Two, stability: run it a few times — same answer? Three, agreement: does the fancy option actually differ, and where? Four, weight: judge the field that drives the decision, not the average. Five, denominator: is the headline padded by trivial cases? Keep the simple default unless the fancy part earns it.

beats.narration_text: Check one — isolate. Same sixty sections, same vocabulary, same interface. The only thing that changes is the backend: a deterministic rule-based matcher, versus a pinned open model — qwen two-point-five, seven billion, temperature zero, on our own hardware. Three runs each. One variable; everything else fixed.

shot.new_visual_element: Two backends side-by-side; 'only this changes' toggle; fixed conditions listed

control.name: rule_based_v1
control.desc: deterministic lexicon matcher · offline · no key

treatment.name: qwen2.5-coder:7b
treatment.desc: pinned open model · temp 0 · self-hosted · digest dae161e27b0e…

show.event: Control card (rule_based_v1) + Treatment card (qwen…) draw in side-by-side
A 'only the backend changes' toggle between them arms
Fixed-conditions list settles beneath (60 · lexicon · interface · K=3 · T4)

beats.narration_text: Check two — stability. Run each three times; do the tags hold? The rule-based backend is exactly reproducible — one-point-oh on every field, byte for byte. The model, even at temperature zero, lands near zero-point-nine-nine. That's not randomness — the drift is GPU floating-point. Exact reproducibility is free with the deterministic backend; the model gets close, never quite there.

shot.new_visual_element: Per-field stability, rule-based (1.000) vs qwen (~0.99) side-by-side dots on a near-1.0 axis

show.event: Two labeled columns; per-field rule-based dots pin exactly at 1.000
qwen dots land just below (0.987–0.996); means row 1.000 vs 0.991
'drift = GPU floating-point, not sampling' note settles

beats.narration_text: Check three — agreement. Field by field, the two mostly diverge in the expected way: on the fuzzy, interpretive fields the model tags more liberally — one to two extra terms — and overlap sits near forty percent. Neither is ground truth; which of those extra tags are signal is exactly what faculty review decides.

shot.new_visual_element: Per-field agreement (Jaccard) bars; materials tall; fuzzy fields ~0.4 with +extra-terms

props.note: fuzzy fields: model adds 1–2 extra terms · neither is ground truth

show.event: Jaccard bars fill per field (labeled with the value)
Fuzzy fields (~0.35–0.46) carry a '+extra terms' tag
'neither is ground truth — faculty review decides' note

beats.narration_text: Check four — weight it. Don't average every field equally; judge the one that drives the decision. Here that's materials — it sets a section's core role downstream. And that's where the two agree most: Jaccard zero-point-eight-nine. Where the call actually matters, the cheap backend and the model substantially agree.

props.point: Highest agreement lands exactly on the load-bearing field.

beats.narration_text: Check five — the denominator. And here you have to be honest. Empty-versus-empty counts as agreement, so sparse fields read high for free. Strip the padding, and materials stability falls from zero-point-nine-nine-six to zero-point-nine-three — on just four sections. The rule-based control stays exactly one-point-oh even here. So materials is directionally encouraging, not yet robust — it needs the denser re-run to defend.

beats.narration_text: So — does the fancy tagger earn it? On this evidence, no: ship the deterministic default. It's exactly reproducible, offline, needs no key, and it agrees with the model where it matters. Keep the model as a named, pinned option for later. And where the two disagree — the fuzzy fields, the difficulty score — that isn't failure; it's the agenda for faculty review. One caveat stays on the record: the strongest number rests on four sections.

props.artifactTitle: Does the Fancy Part Earn It?
artifactLines: Isolate one variable: rule-based vs a pinned open model, everything else fixed.
Stability: rule-based exactly reproducible (1.000); the model near-exact (~0.991, temp 0).
Weighted where it matters — materials — the two agree most (Jaccard 0.89).
Denominator check: that 0.89 rests on n≈4 — verdict stays provisional pending a denser run.
Decision: ship the deterministic default; keep the named, pinned model as an option.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take any simple-versus-fancy choice in your own pipeline and run the five checks: isolate one variable, test stability over a few runs, compare agreement field by field, weight the field that drives your decision — and always report the n behind your headline. Ship the simple default unless the fancy part earns it.
